name: International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions (IFLA)
one_line: Global federation of library associations. It has an AI special interest group, publishes guidance on how libraries should respond strategically to AI, and runs Knowledge Rights 21, its European copyright and AI advocacy programme.
field_lens: Library and information science: access to information, information literacy, collection stewardship. MISFIT: the taxonomy has no library or information-science key, so dem_epistemics (knowledge commons) is the closest.
ai_connection: Advocates for libraries on AI and copyright, and on AI literacy for library users. Knowledge Rights 21, which it runs, is holding an event in October 2026 on copyright and AI in the EU and what comes next.

name: Knowledge Rights 21 (KR21)
one_line: Programme run by IFLA and funded by Arcadia, working with LIBER and SPARC Europe, to reform European copyright so that research, libraries and the public can access and use knowledge, including for text-and-data mining and AI.
field_lens: Library copyright advocacy and research-access law
ai_connection: Has a standing 'Research & AI' topic and policy work on the TDM exceptions and the AI Act. It is holding an event in October 2026 on copyright and AI in the EU and what comes next.

name: Association of Research Libraries (ARL), with the Coalition for Networked Information (CNI): Futurescape Libraries AI Toolkit
one_line: Association of North American research libraries. It has AI principles, AI policy advocacy, and the ARL/CNI scenario-planning toolkit for an AI-shaped future of scholarship.
field_lens: Research librarianship plus scenario planning (futures methods) applied to scholarship and AI. MISFIT: no library key in the taxonomy.
ai_connection: Says it develops principles, does advocacy and uses scenario planning to prepare libraries for AI. With CNI it built the Futurescape Libraries AI Toolkit of reusable activities for planning for AI's consequences, and runs workshops on it nationwide.

name: InterPARES Trust AI
one_line: Multinational, interdisciplinary archival-science research project (2021-2026, led from UBC) on AI that keeps public records trustworthy and available, and on making archival principles inform responsible AI development.
field_lens: Archival science and diplomatics: authenticity, provenance, paradata and chains of custody for records
ai_connection: Its stated goals are the benefits and risks of AI for records and archives and 'ensuring archival principles inform responsible AI'. Outputs include paradata documentation, cryptographic provenance for AI-generated images (IEEE Big Data 2025), AI competencies for archivists, and a June 2026 symposium.

name: Institutional Data Initiative (IDI), Harvard Law School Library
one_line: Research initiative at Harvard Law School Library, grown out of its Library Innovation Lab. It helps libraries and other knowledge institutions refine and publish their collections as data, starting with a large public-domain books dataset for AI.
field_lens: Library stewardship of collections as a public, documented knowledge commons for AI training
ai_connection: Publishes library-stewarded, provenance-documented training data (public-domain books) as an alternative to scraped corpora. Leadership: Greg Leppert, Jonathan Zittrain, Amanda Watson.

name: Transparent Books (HathiTrust, Northeastern University Library and Authors Alliance), successor to the Public Interest Corpus
location: Ann Arbor, MI and Boston, MA, USA
one_line: Five-year Mellon grant (2026-2031, $5M) to build a noncommercial books corpus stewarded by libraries, from HathiTrust's 19M+ volumes, for transparent AI and computational research. It follows the Public Interest Corpus planning project (Dec 2024 - Apr 2026).
field_lens: Research libraries and memory institutions as stewards of training data; author-interest and public-interest copyright
ai_connection: Aims to 'leverage AI for the public good and scholarly discovery', supplying verified, transparent book text for noncommercial research and language models under shared public-interest principles.

name: Authors Alliance
one_line: Nonprofit for authors who want their work widely read. It has standing projects on AI, authorship and the public interest, and on text-and-data mining and fair use.
field_lens: Copyright law and authorship from a public-interest, access-to-knowledge standpoint
ai_connection: Runs 'AI, Authorship, and the Public Interest' and co-founded the Public Interest Corpus and Transparent Books. It analyses AI-training litigation (e.g. the Thomson Reuters v. ROSS appeal, Sept 2026).

name: Software Heritage (incl. CodeCommons)
one_line: Universal archive of source code, hosted by Inria with UNESCO support. CodeCommons, its consortium funded by France 2030, turns the archive into a curated, traceable commons for training code models.
field_lens: Digital preservation and archiving of software as cultural heritage, with archival provenance
ai_connection: CodeCommons requires models trained on the archive to be openly licensed. It offers traceability so builders can respect creators' rights, verification of data inclusion and attribution of generated code, and lets authors opt out.

name: Open Future
one_line: European think tank on the digital commons. Its main AI lines are Public AI, AI and the knowledge commons (Wikimedia, libraries), and transparency of training data.
field_lens: Commons governance and open-movement policy (Ostrom-style commons applied to knowledge infrastructure)
ai_connection: Published a 2025 Public AI white paper and a feasibility study showing European libraries can build a multilingual AI-ready books dataset. Other work: a white paper on Wikimedia and the AI knowledge loop, an Alignment Assembly report, and EU submissions on AI Act training-data transparency and on foundation models as core platform services.

name: Creative Commons: CC signals and AI and the Commons
one_line: Steward of the CC licences. It is developing CC signals, a framework that lets creators and institutions say how AI systems may reuse their work, and publishes guidance on open heritage and licences in the AI era.
field_lens: Open licensing and knowledge-commons norms, with reciprocity
ai_connection: CC signals aims for a 'reciprocal and sustainable AI ecosystem'. Blog posts include 'Guidance on Using CC Licenses in an AI Ecosystem' (Sept 2026), 'Open Heritage in the Age of AI' (Aug 2026) and guidance for Indigenous collections (Sept 2026).

name: COMMUNIA Association for the Public Domain
one_line: European association that advocates for the public domain and for access to culture and knowledge. It has a recurring line of policy papers on machine learning and AI outputs.
field_lens: Public-domain and copyright policy from the cultural-heritage and commons movement
ai_connection: Policy Paper #15 (2023) is on using copyrighted works to train machine learning; Policy Paper #22 (July 2025) argues against new exclusive rights for AI-generated outputs.

name: Open Data Institute (ODI)
one_line: UK nonprofit (founded by Tim Berners-Lee and Nigel Shadbolt) on data stewardship and data institutions. It runs a Data-centric AI programme and event series and data-ethics work for AI.
field_lens: Data stewardship, open data and data institutions (trusts, cooperatives)
ai_connection: Runs the 'DCAI' (data-centric AI) series, e.g. #16 'AI chatbots must not be the new social media' (Oct 2026), and Data Ethics Professionals sessions on AI. It co-launched a global effort on the data foundations AI needs for public services.

name: Starling Lab for Data Integrity (Stanford and USC)
location: Stanford and Los Angeles, CA, USA
one_line: Joint Stanford-USC lab that prototypes tools and principles for trust in digital records: capture, storage and verification of authentic media for journalism, history, law and archives.
field_lens: Archival integrity and authenticity of records, cryptographic provenance, documentary practice
ai_connection: 2026 outputs on deepfakes as evidence, a guide to legislation on synthetic media and content provenance, and AI's effect on documentary truth. Applies archival chain-of-custody to synthetic media.

name: WITNESS
one_line: Human-rights video organisation that helps people use and preserve video as evidence. It runs a sustained deepfakes and AI programme, including regional deepfake rapid-response forces.
field_lens: Human-rights documentation and video-as-evidence practice from the Majority World, including archiving guidance for activists
ai_connection: Launched a deepfake rapid-response force in Brazil (Sept 2026) and a report on verifying what's real after the Nepal floods (Sept 2026). Its mission is to make sure real evidence 'can't be ignored, discredited, or faked'.

name: Center for an Informed Public (CIP), University of Washington
one_line: Centre founded in 2019 by UW's Information School, Human Centered Design & Engineering and School of Law. It researches how misinformation spreads and how people and institutions can navigate information environments.
field_lens: Information science, crisis informatics and collective sensemaking
ai_connection: 2025 study on generative AI chatbots as 'super communicators' that persuade through anthropomorphic appeal. August 2026 work on scrutinising AI science evaluations with 'critically engaged pragmatism'. Also tracks AI-era election rumours.

name: International Panel on the Information Environment (IPIE)
one_line: Independent global science body (500+ experts from 75 countries) modelled on the IPCC, giving scientific assessments of threats to the information environment.
field_lens: Scientific assessment of the information environment, IPCC-style (evidence synthesis and expert surveys)
ai_connection: Runs standing scientific panels on Global Standards for AI Audits, AI and Peacebuilding, and AI and Economic Inclusion, alongside annual expert surveys (Sept 2026).

name: Forum on Information & Democracy
one_line: International body, founded on RSF's initiative and backed by the Partnership for Information and Democracy, that issues policy frameworks for a democratic information space. 'Safeguarding Access to Reliable Information in the Age of AI' is a core workstream.
field_lens: Journalism and information-space governance, multilateral policy
ai_connection: Lists AI and the information space as a core focus (deepfakes, disinformation, trust), with a standing AI workstream. Its earlier policy framework is 'AI as a Public Good'.

name: Oxford Internet Institute (OII)
one_line: Oxford department for the social science of the internet. Its AI groups include Governance of Emerging Technologies, Governing in the Age of AI, Reasoning with Machines, and the Mind and Emerging Technologies Lab.
field_lens: Internet studies, information ethics, law and social data science
ai_connection: Its Governance of Emerging Technologies group works on LLM truthfulness ('careless speech') and tighter LLM regulation, risk management for medical LLMs (July 2025), deepfake generation tools (May 2025) and EU AI Act loopholes.

name: AI Security Initiative, Center for Long-Term Cybersecurity (CLTC), UC Berkeley School of Information
one_line: Programme in Berkeley's School of Information that turns risk-management standards into guidance for frontier and agentic AI. CLTC is on the aisafety.com map; the initiative is not on this roster.
field_lens: Risk management and standards engineering (NIST-style profiles) from an information school
ai_connection: Published a General-Purpose AI Risk-Management Standards Profile (Apr 2026), an Agentic AI Risk-Management Standards Profile (Feb 2026), Intolerable Risk Threshold Recommendations (Feb 2025) and risk thresholds for AI-enabled cyber threats (Jan 2026).

name: Data Provenance Initiative
one_line: Volunteer collective of legal and ML researchers, led by Shayne Longpre with roots at the MIT Media Lab. It audits the licences, sources and consent behind thousands of AI training datasets.
field_lens: Dataset provenance auditing: legal and licensing analysis of the AI data supply chain
ai_connection: Audited 1,800+ text datasets (licences omitted in 68%+, error rates 50%+) and built the Data Provenance Explorer. 'Consent in Crisis' (2024) documented the decline of the AI data commons, as 28%+ of critical C4 sources became restricted.

name: Data Nutrition Project
one_line: Nonprofit, born in the 2018 Harvard/MIT Assembly fellowship and independent since 2021, that makes the Dataset Nutrition Label for checking datasets before AI training.
field_lens: Standardised labelling and documentation (modelled on FDA nutrition labels), with sociotechnical data governance
ai_connection: Offers Dataset Nutrition Labels, labelling as a service, data-governance consulting and training on sociotechnical AI, so dataset quality and provenance are visible before models are built.

name: Research Data Alliance (RDA)
one_line: Global community-driven body for research-data stewardship (FAIR data, data documentation, trusted access). It now has groups on documenting generative AI in research and on access for AI agents.
field_lens: Research data stewardship, FAIR principles and data documentation
ai_connection: Has a 'Documenting Generative AI Interactions in Research' interest group, and the VANTAGE working group on whether AI agents should be given access to restricted research data. Its 2026 AI cross-fertilisation meetings cover trust, governance and FAIR readiness for AI agents.

name: AI4LAM (Artificial Intelligence for Libraries, Archives and Museums)
one_line: International participatory community, with regional chapters and national nodes, on AI 'in, for and by' libraries, archives and museums. It runs the Fantastic Futures conferences (2026 theme 'Trust in the Loop').
field_lens: Cultural-heritage (LAM) practice: metadata, cataloguing, provenance of derivatives
ai_connection: Its Speech-to-Text working group wrote 'Transcript Provenance Metadata Elements' to make AI-generated derivatives transparent and traceable. It also has an AI Literacy working group (Oct 2026).

name: Wikimedia Deutschland: Wikidata Embedding Project
one_line: Wikimedia Deutschland's project, launched October 2025, that opens Wikidata's verified, sourced knowledge to AI builders through a multilingual vector database (with Jina.AI and DataStax).
field_lens: Community-curated knowledge commons (Wikidata) with source transparency
ai_connection: Aims to reduce misinformation in generative AI by grounding it in verified sources, to make sources transparent and to bring in underrepresented knowledge that LLMs miss. The Wikimedia Foundation is on the roster; this German chapter's project is not.

name: Internet Archive
one_line: Nonprofit digital library and the largest public web archive (Wayback Machine). Its own AI engagement is light: copyright and AI submissions, and 2026 essays on access to knowledge in the age of AI.
field_lens: Web archiving and digital library practice
ai_connection: Transferable method: web archiving as a time-stamped, independent record of what was published, a check on provenance and model claims as AI-generated content floods the web. Its AI posts: Copyright Office comments (2023) and 'Open For Whom? Access to Knowledge in the Age of AI' (July 2026).

name: Library Futures (NYU Engelberg Center)
one_line: Project of NYU Law's Engelberg Center on technology, policy and public access to information: digital ownership, library lending rights, and research and advocacy networks.
field_lens: Library rights advocacy and information policy
ai_connection: Transferable method: legal and policy advocacy for the public's rights to access and lend digital knowledge, which could apply to who controls AI-mediated access to knowledge. Its own AI engagement is light (one Dec 2025 piece on algorithmic curation).

name: KB, National Library of the Netherlands
one_line: Dutch national library. It has AI principles (2020) and has changed its terms and put technical barriers in place against commercial AI crawling of its Delpher and DBNL collections, while keeping them open for academic research.
field_lens: National-library collection stewardship and rights management
ai_connection: Transferable method: a public memory institution setting consent and access rules for AI use of national collections, separating research from commercial training, and reviewing them as law and court rulings change.

name: Day of AI (MIT RAISE: Responsible AI for Social Empowerment and Education)
one_line: Free PreK-12 AI literacy curriculum from MIT RAISE (Cynthia Breazeal). It claims 70,000 teachers trained in 175 countries and 4M+ students reached, and launched a grade-by-grade curriculum in August 2026.
field_lens: Education and learning sciences (MISFIT: the taxonomy has no education tradition; closest is child and youth development). Draws on developmental pedagogy and social robotics.
ai_connection: High-school units cover ethics, identity and societal decision-making about AI, deepfakes, bias and privacy. They also cover 'Responsible and Differentiated AI Use', which puts critical thinking ahead of reliance on AI. It is the largest school channel for public AI literacy, though nothing in it is framed as catastrophic risk.

name: TeachAI
one_line: Coalition run with the World Economic Forum (founded by Code.org, ETS, ISTE and Khan Academy) that publishes AI guidance for schools and education policymakers and promotes AI literacy.
field_lens: Education policy and school leadership (MISFIT: education)
ai_connection: It publishes the AI Guidance for Schools Toolkit, Foundational Policy Ideas for education systems, and 2025 briefs with CSTA on computer-science education in the AI era. It is a main source of the AI-use rules that school systems adopt, so it is a lever for norms on student cognitive autonomy.

name: AILit Framework (European Commission and OECD) and the PISA 2029 Media & AI Literacy assessment
one_line: Joint EC-OECD AI literacy framework for primary and secondary education, drafted in May 2025 and revised after consultation with 2,000+ stakeholders. It feeds the innovative domain of PISA 2029.
field_lens: Comparative education policy and international assessment (OECD Directorate for Education and Skills)
ai_connection: Its four domains are Engage, Create, Manage and Shape AI. It asks students to weigh AI's 'opportunities and risks' and keep agency over how AI shapes their lives. Through PISA 2029, students' AI literacy will be measured across dozens of countries, making it the most consequential public-education measurement of how well people can resist AI-driven deskilling and manipulation.

name: Experience AI (Raspberry Pi Foundation with Google DeepMind)
one_line: Free AI literacy curriculum for ages 8-17 from the Raspberry Pi Foundation, built with Google DeepMind. It is used in 180+ countries and won the 2025 UNESCO King Hamad Prize.
field_lens: Computing education research and pedagogy
ai_connection: Its 'AI safety' unit for ages 11-14 (Feb 2026) covers privacy, misinformation, trust and responsibility. A Sept 2026 LLM unit ('think first, prompt second') targets cognitive offloading head-on, so learners keep control of their own learning. It is an unusually direct school-level intervention against deskilling.

name: Digital Promise: AI in education (AI literacy framework, Responsibly Designed AI certification)
one_line: US education-innovation nonprofit, chartered by Congress, with an AI literacy framework, a product certification for edtech AI, and research programmes on AI in learning.
field_lens: Learning sciences, education research and product certification
ai_connection: Its 'Responsibly Designed AI' certification judges edtech tools on educator and learner autonomy, privacy and transparency. Its framework defines AI literacy as critically understanding and evaluating AI, and it insists AI should 'augment, rather than replace' teachers and learners. It is a working certification model for AI that protects human agency.

name: EDSAFE AI Alliance (InnovateEDU)
one_line: Global coalition led by InnovateEDU since 2020, built around the S.A.F.E. principles (Safety, Accountability, Fairness, Efficacy) for AI in education. It has 28 steering organisations, 175+ companies on its Industry Council and 29 district Policy Labs.
field_lens: Education governance, standards and benchmarking (MISFIT: education)
ai_connection: Its SAFE Benchmarks Framework, district Policy Labs and AI fellowships (156 fellows) set norms that edtech companies and school districts must work to. It shows a sector building its own AI safety and accountability standards from the bottom up.

name: News Literacy Project: AI literacy resources
one_line: US nonprofit for news and media literacy (Checkology, RumorGuard, The Sift) that has built a body of AI-literacy material for teachers and the public.
field_lens: News and media literacy education, information-integrity practice
ai_connection: Its classroom resources include 'AI or not?' lessons, '6 Things to Know About AI', the 'Two Truths and AI' video series, RumorGuard debunks of deepfakes and AI slop, and teen safety tips for AI. It teaches the public epistemic self-defence against AI-generated misinformation.

name: Elements of AI (University of Helsinki and MinnaLearn)
one_line: Free MOOC series for non-experts on what AI is and how it affects society, with 2M+ enrolments from 170+ countries. 'Get AI Ready' is a 60-minute AI-literacy course mapped to the EU AI Act.
field_lens: Public and adult education, university outreach
ai_connection: Its course content covers AI's societal impact and ethical risks. The transferable asset is mass adult-education infrastructure in many EU languages that could carry AI-risk and cognitive-autonomy literacy. Today it teaches mostly fundamentals and compliance.

name: KI-Campus (Stifterverband)
one_line: Leading free AI learning platform in the German-speaking world, run by the Stifterverband with federal funding. 190,000+ learners have earned 100,000+ certificates, and it runs teacher courses under 'KI macht Schule'.
field_lens: Higher and adult education, teacher professional development
ai_connection: It offers 'KI-Kompetenzen für Lehrkräfte', courses on explainable AI and LLMs, and EU AI Act essentials, with a new teaching lounge in November 2026. Transferable method: a German-language public AI-literacy infrastructure that reaches universities and teachers and could carry AI-risk content, which it barely covers today.

name: Leaf: 'Dilemmas and Dangers in AI' course
one_line: US 501(c)(3) offering online interdisciplinary courses for teenagers aged 14-19. One of its five courses, 'Dilemmas and Dangers in AI', is about steering advanced AI towards benefit.
field_lens: Secondary and gifted education, humanities-style seminar teaching
ai_connection: It runs five-week, sliding-scale cohorts on AI risk and steering AI; the next runs 12 Oct-20 Nov 2026. It is one of the few programmes that teach AI-risk ideas to school-age students. It is listed on the aisafety.com map but missing from this roster.

name: National Education Association (NEA): AI in Education
one_line: Largest US union (educators, PreK-12 and higher ed). Its AI Task Force report (June 2024) set five principles; it now runs an AI hub with micro-credentials, courses and model school-board policies.
field_lens: Organised labour, teacher professional standards
ai_connection: Its principles keep students and educators central, demand evidence-based AI and data protection, and set 'AI literacy and agency' for all. The task force documented overreliance, AI grading errors, biased surveillance and opaque data governance. It sets union norms for human judgement in high-stakes educational decisions.

name: Education International (EI)
one_line: Global federation of teachers' unions (about 380 member organisations, roughly 32M educators) whose Worlds of Education platform runs a running debate on AI in schools.
field_lens: Organised labour, political economy of education
ai_connection: In September 2026 it published critiques of UNESCO and OECD/EC AI literacy frameworks for turning schools into 'live testing grounds for AI' and sites of data extraction, alongside union pieces on putting AI to use. It is the global teacher-union voice on power and agency in AI's spread through schools. Its formal AI resolution could not be verified (site search blocked).

name: European Trade Union Committee for Education (ETUCE)
one_line: European region of Education International, representing education unions across Europe, now campaigning on AI and education data.
field_lens: Organised labour, EU social dialogue
ai_connection: In September 2026 its 'Students are not for Data Mining' campaign, part of Stop the Omnibus, urged EU states to reject a proposal letting Big Tech train AI on students' and educators' data. It wrote an open letter on GDPR Article 88bis and in October 2026 documented union practice that treats AI pilots as collaborative professional development. It is organised-labour counter-power on AI training data in a sector with vulnerable data subjects.

name: Chartered College of Teaching
one_line: Professional body for teachers in England. It runs the government-funded 'Safe and effective use of AI in education' course and assessment, developed with Chiltern Learning Trust.
field_lens: Teacher professionalism, evidence-informed practice
ai_connection: It runs an updated, free course and assessment for teachers on the safe and effective use of AI. It is the main professional-formation channel through which England's teachers learn to judge AI's effect on learning.

name: Cognitive Resonance (Benjamin Riley)
one_line: Small venture that teaches educators and policymakers about generative AI through cognitive science, 'Building Human Knowledge to Halt AI Hype', with workshops, white papers and talks.
field_lens: Cognitive science of learning
ai_connection: Its method has two steps: first explain how human cognition and learning work, then how LLMs produce output. Teachers can then judge where AI undermines effortful thinking. Its framing is critical and deflationary, and it is one of the few outfits that bring learning science explicitly to bear on AI.

name: Stanford SCALE Initiative: AI Hub for Education
one_line: Stanford Graduate School of Education initiative bridging research and practice. Its AI Hub for Education published 'The Evidence Base on AI in K-12: A 2026 Review' of causal studies.
field_lens: Education research methods, causal evaluation
ai_connection: It builds the causal evidence base on whether AI tools improve or erode student and educator outcomes, which any claim about AI deskilling in schools needs. Its emphasis is on efficacy rather than harm.

name: SLATE: Centre for the Science of Learning & Technology, with the AI LEARN centre (University of Bergen)
one_line: Norway's national centre for learning analytics, combining information science, cognitive science, pedagogy, sociology and law. It now hosts AI LEARN, a five-year centre on human-AI interaction in learning led by Barbara Wasson.
field_lens: Learning analytics, learning sciences, cognitive science
ai_connection: It researches students' cognitive engagement with generative AI, young people's trust in AI and human agency in AI-driven education. It also launched three master's courses on human-AI interaction (May 2026) and runs the NOKI national AI Olympiad for secondary schools.

name: Leibniz-Institut für Wissensmedien (IWM)
one_line: Leibniz institute in Tübingen researching how people use digital media and AI to learn, find information and share knowledge. It has a Language and AI in Education lab.
field_lens: Educational and cognitive psychology of knowledge media
ai_connection: Recent work includes a doctoral thesis on 'When and how do we decide to use AI?' (Aug 2026), which addresses offloading decisions, and an AI masterclass for teachers (Aug 2026). Its experimental psychology of knowledge acquisition could anchor research on cognitive offloading to AI.

name: Centre for Research in Digital Education (University of Edinburgh)
one_line: Edinburgh Futures Institute / Moray House centre for critical research on digital education, AI and education futures, home to Ben Williamson's work on edtech platforms and datafication.
field_lens: Critical data studies, sociology of education
ai_connection: It does critical research on generative AI in education, including a Sept 2026 review of the evidence by Judy Robertson and Ben Williamson. It analyses the political economy of AI platforms in schools and universities.

name: Civics of Technology Project
one_line: Community of teachers and education researchers (Daniel Krutka, Marie Heath) promoting critical inquiry into technology in K-16 classrooms, with curricula, a conference and a newsletter.
field_lens: Media ecology (Postman), STS, social-studies education
ai_connection: Its 2026 output includes research on refusing educational AI ('critical optimism'), lessons on 'What is AI made of?', students investigating data centres, technofeudalism, and rethinking educators' roles beyond 'human-in-the-loop'. It brings critical technology pedagogy into teacher practice.

name: Deans for Impact
one_line: US nonprofit of teacher-preparation leaders that translates cognitive science ('The Science of Learning') into teacher training. In August 2026 it announced an AI framework for teacher preparation with TeachingWorks.
field_lens: Cognitive science of learning, teacher education
ai_connection: Its AI framework for teacher preparation was announced in August 2026. Transferable method: turning cognitive-science findings on effortful retrieval and practice into teacher norms, which is what guarding against AI-induced cognitive offloading requires.

name: Harvard Embedded EthiCS
one_line: Collaboration between philosophers and computer scientists that embeds ethics modules in Harvard computer science courses. It is a model copied by other universities, and demand surged with AI use (Harvard Gazette, Nov 2025).
field_lens: Philosophy and applied ethics pedagogy
ai_connection: Philosophers teach modules on trust in AI, algorithmic fairness, AI art, content moderation and big-tech regulation inside technical courses. It is an established method for building normative judgement into the people who build AI. Explicit AI-safety or alignment modules could not be confirmed.

name: AI Safety, Ethics and Society course and textbook (Center for AI Safety)
one_line: Dan Hendrycks's textbook (Routledge) and free virtual course for students and practitioners, including non-computer-scientists. The latest cohort ran Nov 2025-Feb 2026.
field_lens: Safety engineering, complex systems, game theory, international relations, ethics
ai_connection: The course is built on non-ML disciplines: safety-engineering risk decomposition, complex-systems theory, game theory of races, moral uncertainty and governance. It is the main AI-safety curriculum designed for audiences outside computer science. CAIS itself is not on the roster.

name: AAC&U Institute on AI, Pedagogy, and the Curriculum
one_line: Seven-month team-based institute run by the American Association of Colleges and Universities. 316 teams from 296 institutions have taken part; the current cohort runs 10 Sept 2026-6 Apr 2027.
field_lens: Liberal education, curriculum design in higher education
ai_connection: Teams 'examine the ethical and equity implications of AI' and write AI competencies and literacies into course and programme learning outcomes. It is the broadest channel for reshaping non-CS university curricula around AI.

name: AI Pedagogy Project (metaLAB (at) Harvard)
one_line: Project incubated at metaLAB (at) Harvard in 2023, within the Berkman Klein Center (already on the map). It curates open AI assignments and guides for educators, used in 162 countries and recommended by 134+ colleges.
field_lens: Digital humanities, arts-based critical pedagogy
ai_connection: Its hands-on assignments for humanities classes get students to probe AI's capabilities and limits, for example by critiquing AI summaries, comparing human and machine critique, and examining AI images in misinformation. Its 2026 events include the AI & Tell dialogue series and a public AI summit for educators.

name: CRAFT: Classroom-Ready Resources About AI For Teaching (Stanford)
one_line: Stanford GSE and HAI initiative that co-designs free, multidisciplinary high-school lessons on AI with teachers, for art, maths, English and history classes.
field_lens: Humanistic and interdisciplinary curriculum design
ai_connection: Its lessons ask students to 'explore, understand, question, and critique AI' across subjects, which places AI literacy in humanities classrooms rather than only computer science. No 2025-26 dated activity was visible.

name: Spencer Foundation: AI and Education Initiative
one_line: Leading US education-research funder whose AI and Education Initiative, launched after a spring 2024 convening, funds research on AI and learning, AI policy, AI ethics and justice, and AI-transformed research methods.
field_lens: Education research funding, equity
ai_connection: It funds evidence-based guidance 'that centers the needs of young people'. Its questions include whether inequities are 'disrupted or reinforced with/through AI', and it accepts AI work across all of its grant programmes. It is a funder that new AI-safety funders could co-fund with on AI's effects on learning.

name: Division of Digital Psychiatry, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center / Harvard Medical School (John Torous), incl. MindBench.ai
one_line: Clinical digital-psychiatry group that has become one of the most prolific evaluators of LLM chatbot harms to mental health.
field_lens: Clinical psychiatry and digital mental health; trial methodology; clinical validation
ai_connection: Built MindBench.ai with NAMI (Nov 2025), a platform that rates LLM mental-health tools on profile and clinical reasoning. Published a functional typology of LLM-associated psychotic phenomena (Lancet Digital Health, Apr 2026), a scoping review of LLM chatbot mental-health harms such as sycophancy and crisis failures (npj Digit Med, Aug 2026), a psychiatric-crisis guardrail and dataset (Apr 2026), simulation-based estimation of LLM risk (BMJ Ment Health, 2026), 'Mental Health AI Chatbots as Pharmakon' (2026) and a JAMA piece on mental-health AI safety (Jul 2026). The pharmacological and trial-design framing is the closest thing to a toxicology-style approach that I found.

name: Department of Affective Disorders, Aarhus University Hospital – Psychiatry / Aarhus University (Søren Dinesen Østergaard group)
one_line: Psychiatric-epidemiology group that predicted chatbot-induced delusions in 2023 and then documented cases in psychiatric health records.
field_lens: Psychiatric epidemiology using register and electronic-health-record data
ai_connection: Screened the health records of the Central Denmark Region psychiatric services for mentions of chatbots or ChatGPT. Found 38 patients with potentially harmful consequences, most often worsening or consolidation of delusions (Acta Psychiatr Scand, Feb 2026). Published papers on emotion contagion and mania (2025) and on the adverse effects of voice-based chatbots (2026). An editorial asked 'have we learned nothing from the global social media experiment?' (2026), and it co-authored with KCL on trajectory-based chatbot safety assessment (JMIR Ment Health, 2026). This is EHR-based harm surveillance, the method a public-health approach to AI needs.

name: Department of Psychosis Studies, Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience, King's College London (Hamilton Morrin, Thomas Pollak)
one_line: Psychosis researchers who describe the mechanisms of AI-associated delusions and safeguards against them.
field_lens: Clinical psychosis research and neuropsychiatry
ai_connection: Lead paper in The Lancet Psychiatry (2026) on AI-associated delusions: the risks, how LLMs co-create delusions, and safeguarding strategies, followed by a terminology debate in the journal. Also a BMC Psychiatry case report of delusions corroborated by a chatbot (2026), 'Characterizing the spiral' (NPP Digital Psychiatry, 2026), and, with Aarhus, a call to assess chatbot mental-health safety over conversation trajectories rather than single end points (JMIR Ment Health, Apr 2026). The trajectory method maps onto multi-turn sycophancy evaluations.

name: RAND Health Care (Ryan McBain, Jonathan Cantor and colleagues): generative AI and mental health research
location: Santa Monica, CA / Washington, DC, USA
one_line: Health-services and population-survey research on how often young people turn to chatbots for mental health and how LLMs answer suicide queries.
field_lens: Health services research, survey epidemiology, suicide prevention
ai_connection: Population prevalence work: generative AI use for mental-health advice among US adolescents and young adults (JAMA Netw Open, Nov 2025), chatbot use and disclosure for mental health (JAMA Pediatrics, Aug 2026), and how often mental health comes up in public generative-AI conversation logs (JAMA Netw Open, Aug 2026; NIMH R01-funded). Evaluation work: comparisons of LLM and clinician suicide-risk judgements (Psychiatric Services 2025; JMIR 2025) and a paper on making medical AI benchmarks clinically interpretable (BMJ Ment Health, Sep 2026). In effect these are third-party, epidemiology-grade evaluations of frontier-model behaviour. Note: RAND's AI-security work is mainstream AI policy, and this entry is only its health unit.

name: Flinders Health and Medical Research Institute, Flinders University (Ashley Hopkins, Bradley Menz, Michael Sorich): AI vigilance and health-disinformation safeguards
one_line: Clinical-epidemiology group that repeatedly tests frontier LLMs' safeguards against producing health disinformation and other harmful health content.
field_lens: Clinical and cancer epidemiology, pharmacology, public health
ai_connection: Ran repeated cross-sectional audits of LLM safeguards against health disinformation (BMJ 2024), called for 'AI vigilance' ('Weapons of Mass Disinformation', JAMA Intern Med 2024), and showed that system instructions can turn LLMs into health-disinformation chatbots (Annals of Internal Medicine, 2025). Followed with a cross-sectional evaluation of consumer LLM platforms (JMIR Infodemiology, 2026) and a test of generative image and video safeguards against content harmful to public health (Public Health Reports, 2026). The method is surveillance-style repeated measurement of model safeguards, a public-health version of misuse evaluation.

name: Mind (mental health charity): Mental Health in the Age of AI Commission
one_line: The large mental-health charity for England and Wales, which in July 2026 launched a 12-month commission into AI and mental health.
field_lens: Population mental health, lived experience, mental-health advocacy
ai_connection: On 9 July 2026 Mind formally launched a 12-month 'Commission into AI and mental health', warning about the rise in people using AI rather than traditional services for mental-health support. It is a standing campaign under 'Mental health in the age of AI'. This brings a lived-experience, population-mental-health inquiry model to consumer AI. I could not read the commission page itself (HTTP 403), so chair, members and remit are unconfirmed.

name: Center for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH): AI chatbot safety testing
one_line: Digital-harms watchdog that runs persona-based safety tests of chatbots, such as 'Fake Friend' on ChatGPT and teens.
field_lens: Civil-society auditing of online harms; adolescent safety
ai_connection: 'Fake Friend' (Aug 2025) ran 60 harmful prompts as teen personas and got 1,200 ChatGPT responses: 53% contained dangerous content on self-harm, suicide planning, eating disorders and substance use, and simple framing bypassed safeguards. CCDH also has AI work on deepfakes, AI-assisted planning of mass violence, and child safety. This is reproducible harm surveillance in a quasi-toxicological 'exposure test' style.

name: KFF Health Information and Trust initiative (polling and The Monitor)
location: San Francisco, CA / Washington, DC, USA
one_line: Health-policy research organisation that tracks how the public uses and trusts AI for health information, alongside health misinformation.
field_lens: Public-opinion survey research; health communication and misinformation monitoring
ai_connection: Its polling dashboard (updated Jul 2026) tracks 'use of news, social media, and AI for health-related information'. About 35 items in the initiative are tagged Artificial Intelligence. A Sep 2026 analysis covers AI-generated health answers and what happens when people skip the original sources. This is population-level surveillance of the AI-mediated health information environment, a public-health input to sensemaking work.

name: Algorithmovigilance programme, Vanderbilt University Medical Center (Peter Embí, Megan Salwei)
one_line: Biomedical informatics team that moved pharmacovigilance into 'algorithmovigilance', ongoing post-deployment monitoring of AI systems.
field_lens: Pharmacovigilance, clinical informatics, human factors
ai_connection: Coined algorithmovigilance and now runs a deployed AI monitoring and operations system at VUMC ('Design and Early Evaluation of an Algorithmovigilance System', May 2026). Also published on calibrating clinician trust in AI (JAMIA, Aug 2026). The transferable method is the drug-safety model of post-market adverse-event surveillance applied to deployed AI, which is the toxicology and pharmacovigilance template for AI incident monitoring.

name: WHO Health Ethics & Governance unit: Ethics and governance of AI for health (guidance on large multi-modal models)
one_line: The World Health Organization's ethics team, which writes WHO's governance guidance for generative AI in health.
field_lens: Global public health; bioethics and health governance
ai_connection: Published 'Ethics and governance of AI for health: guidance on large multi-modal models' (98 pp., current version dated 25 March 2025), which sets governance expectations for developing and deploying generative models across health care and public health. WHO's other 2025-26 AI output is mostly AI as a tool, plus GI-AI4H and WHO Europe health-system readiness. I found no WHO programme on the population mental-health harms of consumer chatbots.

name: US FDA Digital Health Advisory Committee: generative-AI mental-health devices
one_line: FDA's expert committee on digital health, which in November 2025 met on generative-AI-enabled digital mental-health medical devices.
field_lens: Public-health regulation; medical-device safety and post-market surveillance
ai_connection: Its 6 Nov 2025 meeting asked how to regulate generative-AI mental-health devices: therapy-like chatbots, their risks and monitoring. A public docket (FDA-2025-N-2338) stayed open to Dec 2025. This applies device-regulation and post-market adverse-event methods to chatbots in mental health. It covers only products marketed as medical devices, not general-purpose chatbots.

name: Global Centre for Preventive Health and Nutrition (GLOBE), Institute for Health Transformation, Deakin University (Kathryn Backholer)
one_line: Commercial-determinants-of-health centre that monitors digital marketing to young people and has started to frame chatbot advertising as a public-health risk.
field_lens: Public health; commercial determinants of health; digital marketing surveillance
ai_connection: Lancet Comment (May 2026): 'Targeted advertising in generative AI chatbots: a new public health risk'. Also evaluated early effects of Australia's Social Media Minimum Age Act (BMJ, Jun 2026) and built SCANNER, a deep-learning system that detects digital marketing of food and alcohol (2026). The transferable method is commercial-determinants analysis and marketing surveillance, the tobacco and alcohol playbook, applied to chatbot monetisation. AI engagement so far is one paper.

name: ISACA: AI audit, risk and security credentials (AAIA, AAIR, AAISM)
one_line: The global IT-audit and governance professional body (home of CISA and COBIT). It now runs AI-specific audit, risk and security credentials, billing AAIA as the world's first advanced AI audit certification.
field_lens: IT audit, internal control and governance frameworks (COBIT), professional certification of auditors
ai_connection: AAIA certifies experienced auditors in AI governance and risk, AI operations, and AI audit tools and techniques. Only people already holding CISA, CIA, CPA, ACCA or chartered-accountant credentials can sit it. Sibling credentials are AAIR (AI risk) and AAISM (AI security management). Together they amount to a standing programme to professionalise the people who audit AI systems.

name: The Institute of Internal Auditors (IIA): AI Auditing Framework
one_line: The global standard-setter and professional body for internal audit. It owns the Global Internal Audit Standards and the Three Lines Model, and publishes a principles-based AI Auditing Framework.
field_lens: Internal audit, the Three Lines Model, governance, risk and control assurance
ai_connection: The AI Auditing Framework was updated in September 2024 with more on generative AI and LLMs, ethics and transparency, and board oversight, plus a practitioner checklist aligned with the Three Lines Model. AI-safety governance research already borrows the IIA's model: Schuett, 'Three lines of defense against risks from AI' (GovAI, 2023). That makes the IIA a natural source for oversight structures at AI labs.

name: International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (IAASB): Technology Position
one_line: The independent global standard-setter for audit and assurance engagements (ISAs, ISAE 3000, ISSA 5000), working under public-interest oversight. It has a Technology Position and a technology quality-management workstream.
field_lens: Assurance standard-setting: evidence, professional scepticism, independence, quality management
ai_connection: In June 2025 it started a workstream on how AI affects audit and assurance quality management, with non-authoritative materials approved in December 2025. Version 3 of its Catalog of Issues (July 2026) adds 'potential new or evolving assurance engagements'. Its AI work so far is about AI used inside audits. Transferable method: generic assurance standards (ISAE 3000, and ISSA 5000 for sustainability) are a ready template for independent, standards-based third-party assurance of AI systems and of AI-lab safety claims.

name: ForHumanity: Independent Audit of AI Systems
one_line: A 501(c)(3) public charity, founded by Ryan Carrier after 25 years in finance, that crowd-sources binary audit criteria for AI systems and trains and certifies independent AI auditors (FHCA). This sits close to compliance training.
field_lens: Financial audit and reporting as institutional model, risk management, certification
ai_connection: It says it builds 'an infrastructure of trust predicated on the 50+ year track record of financial accounting and reporting'. Its Independent Audit of AI Systems copies the third-party financial-audit set-up: public criteria, certified auditors, independent certification. It covers ethics, bias, privacy, trust and cybersecurity, plus EU AI Act and risk-management schemes. Courses were still running in 2026.

name: Institute and Faculty of Actuaries (IFoA): AI and emerging technologies
one_line: The UK chartered actuarial profession. It publishes an AI Manifesto arguing that involving a Chartered Actuary makes AI 'safer, more robust', ethical and professional guidance on data science and AI, and an ongoing blog line on AI.
field_lens: Actuarial science: model risk management, long-horizon risk quantification, professional standards
ai_connection: Outputs: Ethical and Professional Guidance on Data Science and AI (v2.1, July 2025); a 2023 Risk Alert on AI techniques and outputs; the AI Manifesto; 2026 posts from its Professionalism, Regulation and Ethics Working Party, which argue LLMs should face the same governance controls as actuarial models. Its knowledge of model governance and long-horizon solvency risk could carry over to AI risk. It is in London (int/a hub).

name: International Actuarial Association (IAA): Artificial Intelligence Task Force
location: Ottawa, Canada (global federation of actuarial associations)
one_line: The global federation of actuarial associations. Its AI Task Force works on actuaries' role in identifying and managing the risks of designing and using AI, and engages supranational bodies on AI governance.
field_lens: Actuarial science and professionalism: risk identification, governance, ethics
ai_connection: The AITF ran five workstreams in 2024 (professionalism, ethics, education, governance, innovation; consolidated deliverables published) and four in 2025/26 (engagement, research, case studies and tools, adoption frameworks). The IAA adopted a Statement of Intent on AI, and held AI Summits in Singapore (2024) and San Francisco (February 2025).

name: Society of Actuaries (SOA) Research Institute: AI research
one_line: The largest North American actuarial body. Its Research Institute publishes a regular Actuarial Intelligence Bulletin and AI reports on model governance, ethics and fairness.
field_lens: Actuarial research: model governance, fairness in insurance pricing, mortality and longevity modelling
ai_connection: 2026 outputs: 'Model Governance/Ethics for GenAI Models – Practical Guide and Educational Handbook', and a fairness-framework study of AI in long-term-care insurance pricing. The Actuarial Intelligence Bulletin is recurring. Earlier essay collections looked at AI's effects on mortality, longevity and retirement. This is a standing research line applying actuarial model governance to generative AI.

name: Casualty Actuarial Society (CAS): Research Paper Series on Bias and Insurance
one_line: The property-casualty actuarial body. Its research series, begun in 2022 as 'Race and Insurance Pricing', now covers algorithmic bias and fairness across insurance operations.
field_lens: Actuarial pricing science, quantitative fairness and discrimination testing
ai_connection: Recent papers include 'Regulatory Perspectives on Algorithmic Bias and Unfair Discrimination', 'Comparison of Regulatory Framework for Non-Discriminatory AI Usage in Insurance' (China, US, Canada, Europe), a scalable toolbox for exposing indirect discrimination in rates, and practitioner guides to measuring and mitigating bias. These are measurement methods transferable to auditing AI decision systems.

name: Actuaries Institute (Australia): AI risk management and discrimination guidance
one_line: The Australian actuarial profession. It produced an AI risk-management framework for financial services with the UTS Human Technology Institute, and earlier co-wrote AI-discrimination guidance with the Australian Human Rights Commission.
field_lens: Actuarial risk quantification and controls; anti-discrimination law applied to underwriting
ai_connection: The framework with UTS HTI is organised around four questions: governance (who is accountable), classification, quantification of AI risk, and controls for common use cases. Its December 2022 guidance with the AHRC explains how federal anti-discrimination law applies to AI in insurance pricing and underwriting. It also publishes regular GenAI pieces (Sept–Oct 2026). The HTI framework's publication date was not shown on the page.

name: Armilla AI
one_line: A Lloyd's coverholder selling purpose-built liability insurance and performance warranties for generative AI and AI agents. It underwrites them with independent model evaluations.
field_lens: Insurance underwriting and actuarial risk pricing, third-party verification
ai_connection: Its affirmative AI liability cover (written by Lloyd's underwriters) covers model errors, output liability, agent mistakes and regulatory violations. Policies come with independent verification of AI systems and an AI Risk Hub with a litigation database. It uses insurance pricing as a market incentive for safer AI, similar to AIUC, which is already on the map.

name: Munich Re aiSure (AI performance insurance)
one_line: A product line of the reinsurer Munich Re, insuring AI systems since 2018 against underperformance, hallucination, discrimination, IP and privacy failures.
field_lens: Reinsurance and actuarial pricing of model-performance risk
ai_connection: aiSure covers contractual liabilities, own losses and legal liabilities from AI failures. Munich Re has a dedicated senior underwriter for AI risk. It is the longest-running attempt to price AI model error actuarially, treating AI as probabilistic and its failures as systematic until fixed: a working example of insurance as AI assurance.

name: Financial Stability Board (FSB): AI and financial stability
one_line: The G20 body that coordinates financial regulators. It monitors AI's financial-stability risks, and its Chair warned in August 2026 about frontier AI models.
field_lens: Macroprudential policy, systemic-risk monitoring, international regulatory coordination
ai_connection: On 31 August 2026 FSB Chair Andrew Bailey warned of frontier models' growing autonomy and threat capabilities, mainly for cyber, and called for 'safe and responsible model release and deployment'. In June 2026 the FSB consulted on 12 sound practices for responsible AI adoption. This builds on its 2017 assessment and 2024 update. Its concerns are third-party concentration, correlated models and opacity as a macro-level risk.

name: Bank for International Settlements (BIS) and its Financial Stability Institute: AI work
one_line: The central banks' bank. It has a sustained AI publication line, from its 2024 Annual Economic Report chapter on AI to a 2026 FSI paper on frontier-AI cyber threats to finance.
field_lens: Central banking, macro-financial stability, prudential supervision
ai_connection: Three outputs: the AER 2024 Chapter III 'AI and the economy', on third-party dependency, algorithmic herding and concentration; FSI Insights 63 (December 2024) on regulating AI in finance; FSI Occasional Paper 28, 'When machines attack: frontier AI cyber threats and policy responses in the financial sector' (September 2026). The last says frontier models can 'autonomously identify critical vulnerabilities, develop effective exploits'. It also builds a central-bank community of practice on AI.

name: Bank of England: Financial Policy Committee AI monitoring and the AI Consortium
one_line: The UK central bank. Its Financial Policy Committee monitors AI as a systemic risk, and since May 2025 it has co-run a public-private AI Consortium with the FCA.
field_lens: Macroprudential policy, systemic-risk surveillance, stress testing
ai_connection: The April 2025 Financial Stability in Focus on AI covers correlated AI trading, concentration in AI providers, cyber risk and agentic AI. The AI Consortium, launched 2 May 2025 with the FCA, has met regularly (minutes through June 2026). The July 2026 FSR says rapid progress in frontier AI 'present[s] a significant increase in the risks to financial stability from cyber and operational vulnerabilities' and flags AI-related valuations and credit build-up. It is in London (int/a hub).

name: European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB): Advisory Scientific Committee report on AI and systemic risk
one_line: The EU's macroprudential oversight body. Its Advisory Scientific Committee report No 16, 'Artificial intelligence and systemic risk' (December 2025), maps how AI features amplify systemic financial risk.
field_lens: Macroprudential theory: liquidity mismatch, common exposures, interconnectedness, substitutability, leverage
ai_connection: The report, by Cecchetti, Lumsdaine, Peltonen and Sánchez Serrano, ranks the AI features that worsen systemic risk: monitoring difficulty, concentration, model uniformity, overreliance and excess trust, speed, and opacity or concealment. It discusses AI externalities, regulation and supervision. It is a single flagship report, so the ring is potential. Transferable method: the macroprudential systemic-risk toolkit (surveillance, concentration limits, circuit-breakers) as a template for system-level AI risk governance.

name: Systemic Risk Centre, London School of Economics: AI and financial crises
one_line: An LSE research centre on systemic financial risk. Jón Danielsson and Andreas Uthemann have built a 2025 publication line arguing that AI makes financial crises faster and more severe.
field_lens: Financial economics of systemic risk, endogenous risk and crisis dynamics
ai_connection: Outputs: 'Artificial intelligence and financial crises' (Journal of Financial Stability, August 2025; Discussion Paper 133), and opinion pieces on AI and stability and on how central banks and authorities should respond (February, May and November 2025). The mechanism: speed, shared data and models, strategic complementarities and opacity amplify crises. Proposed responses include authorities' own AI systems, AI-to-AI communication and monitoring. It is in London (int/a hub).

name: Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS): FEAT principles, Veritas and AI risk-management guidelines
one_line: Singapore's central bank and financial regulator. It created the FEAT principles and the open-source Veritas assessment toolkit, and in November 2025 consulted on sector-wide AI risk-management guidelines.
field_lens: Financial supervision, model risk management, industry-consortium standard-building
ai_connection: Veritas (2018–2023, 25+ institutions) produced fairness, ethics, accountability and transparency assessment methods and an open-source toolkit for credit, marketing, underwriting and fraud models. Consultation P017-2025 (13 November 2025 to 31 January 2026) proposes AI risk-management oversight, policies, lifecycle controls and capabilities for all financial institutions, aligned with AI Verify. It shows a regulator building assurance methods with industry.

name: Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) AI Lab: AI Live Testing
one_line: The UK conduct regulator's AI programme. It runs AI Live Testing, in which firms test AI systems in live markets under supervision, alongside a Supercharged Sandbox, an AI Sprint and an AI Input Zone.
field_lens: Conduct regulation, regulatory sandboxes and supervised live testing
ai_connection: AI Live Testing is in its second cohort (testing from April 2026). The Supercharged Sandbox's first cohort had 23 firms. The AI Sprint (January 2025) brought together innovators, academics and consumer representatives. The AI Input Zone (May–June 2026) collected examples of good and poor AI practice. Supervised live testing is a regulatory template that could carry over to evaluating deployed AI. Much of the programme is about enabling adoption. It is in London (int/a hub).

name: Finance Watch: AI in finance
one_line: A public-interest counterweight to the financial lobby in EU policy. It has a 2024–25 line of reports and consultation responses on AI in finance, accountability and consumer protection.
field_lens: Public-interest financial regulation, consumer protection, counter-lobbying
ai_connection: Outputs: 'Artificial intelligence in finance: how to trust a black box?' (March 2025), on conflicts between AI use and the regulatory principles of accountability, responsibility and transparency; 'Protecting EU consumers in the age of AI-driven retail finance' (July 2025); and consultation responses on AI in insurance (June 2025) and on supervising AI in finance (September 2024).

name: Soka Gakkai International (SGI): autonomous weapons and AI–nuclear advocacy
one_line: A worldwide lay Buddhist organisation in the Nichiren tradition, based in Tokyo. It has campaigned against autonomous weapons since 2018 and supports faith-led work on AI and nuclear risk.
field_lens: Nichiren Buddhism (respect for the dignity of life), peace and disarmament advocacy at the UN
ai_connection: SGI has been a member of Stop Killer Robots since 2018. In 2021 it signed the interfaith 'Plea for Preserving Our Shared Humanity' with the WCC, and it has made repeated statements at CCW and UN meetings. On 23 July 2026, ahead of the CCW's Seventh Review Conference, its Global Perspectives Committee called for a treaty on autonomous weapons, a ban on systems that target humans, and meaningful human control. It was one of 12 supporting organisations of the Vatican-hosted Global Nobel Laureates Assembly (14–16 July 2026), where it spoke in the session 'Faith and the Future of Humanity in the Age of AI and Nuclear Weapons' and signed the Rome Declaration on AI, nuclear and autonomous weapons. Toda Peace Institute, which SGI founded, is already on the roster; SGI itself is not.

name: Kyoto University Institute for the Future of Human Society (Kumagai lab): BuddhaBot, BuddhaBot-Plus and Buddharoid
one_line: Prof. Seiji Kumagai's group at Kyoto University, working with the Kyoto start-ups Teraverse and XNOVA, builds Buddhist AI: a scripture-trained dialogue model, augmented-reality apps and a humanoid 'robot monk'. It treats the risks of these systems as an ethics question (ELSI).
field_lens: Buddhist studies; Japanese Buddhist robotics; 'Traditional Knowledge Tech' that brings religious and philosophical traditions into AI
ai_connection: The group released BuddhaBot, a Buddhist dialogue AI, in March 2021 and the Terra Platform AR app in 2022. BuddhaBot-Plus is a GPT-based model trained on Buddhist scriptures. In February 2026 it unveiled Buddharoid at Shoren-in temple, Kyoto: a humanoid robot running that model. The team says it is 'conducting ongoing discussions on ELSI' about the benefits and risks of giving Buddhist AI a body. It plans further 'philosophical AI humanoid robots' that represent philosophers and saints. The work is a sustained test case of how a living tradition builds value-laden AI and decides what an AI may do in religious roles.

name: World Institute for Science, Religion and Culture (WISR; formerly the Center for Christogenesis)
one_line: Ilia Delio's Teilhardian institute, renamed in 2026. Its mission now includes cultivating 'a new way of knowing for an AI age' and an ethics grounded in complexity and evolution.
field_lens: Teilhard de Chardin's evolutionary Christian mysticism, process theology, complexity thought, and contemplative formation
ai_connection: AI runs through its 2026 work. Essays by Delio include 'Intelligence Was Never the Point: Interior to Interiority in the Age of AI' (Aug 2026), 'What the Machine Cannot Know: Reclaiming Education as Spiritual Formation in an Age of AI' (Jul 2026) and 'Connection Is Not Communion' (Sep 2026). Its Hunger for Wholeness podcast has run episodes with Robert Geraci on apocalyptic AI and a 'global mind'. It has held events on Teilhard and AI, interfaith perspectives on AI, and Pope Leo's AI encyclical Magnifica Humanitas. Its 10th-anniversary conference is on 9–11 Nov 2026 at Villanova. It does not use the technical alignment frame: it treats AI as a mirror for collective consciousness and personhood. Under rule B1, a Teilhardian body goes to Contemplative.

name: International Association of Jesuit Universities (IAJU): Task Force on Artificial Intelligence
one_line: The global network of Jesuit universities, founded in 2018 and based in Rome. AI is one of its strategic priorities, run by a seven-member task force that connects AI adoption to Ignatian discernment and cura personalis.
field_lens: Jesuit and Ignatian spirituality (discernment, cura personalis, magis), Catholic social teaching, higher education
ai_connection: The AI Task Force is chaired by Renato Cerqueira and has members from the US, Colombia, Belgium, Spain, India and Japan. It runs a curated knowledge hub, a virtual community of practice for faculty and students, and pilot projects and working groups. Its brief covers governance, teaching and ethical questions about AI. In March–April 2026 it held a symposium, 'The AI Frontier and the Distinctives of Global Jesuit Higher Education', where the Jesuit Curia's Secretariat for Higher Education called AI 'a new frontier'. In July 2026 the Society of Jesus held a week-long conference in Florence on AI and Jesuit formation; that work is related but separate. The frame is education and human dignity, not catastrophic risk.

name: America Media (America: The Jesuit Review)
one_line: The US Jesuit magazine and media ministry. It covers AI steadily, including AI catastrophe and alignment, from a Catholic and Ignatian standpoint.
field_lens: Jesuit journalism, Catholic social teaching, Ignatian spirituality
ai_connection: Recent pieces include editor Sam Sawyer SJ's 'How to worry about A.I. without despairing' (2 Oct 2026). It takes on existential-risk estimates and argues that the alignment problem is a moral question as well as a technical one. Others are Colleen Dulle's report on Pope Leo saying he is not 'in panic mode' about an AI catastrophe but 'we can't just sit back' (28 Sep 2026), a piece on medieval intellectual virtue and AI (Aug 2026), and a live Zoom panel on the reception of Magnifica Humanitas (Aug 2026). It is a sustained faith-media channel that brings AI-risk framing to a large Catholic readership. It could arguably be bridge, given its explicit catastrophic-risk and alignment coverage.

name: Yaqeen Institute for Islamic Research
one_line: A large US Muslim research and education institute. In 2026 it published an Islamic ethical and juristic framework for AI.
field_lens: Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh al-muwazanat, the jurisprudence of balancing; maqasid al-shari'a), Islamic ethics
ai_connection: 'Toward an Islamic Ethics and Fiqh of Artificial Intelligence' (AbuTaleb, Alkiek, Hani, Ansari and Khan) was published on 12 June 2026 and updated on 30 September 2026. It argues for proactive ethical assessment at the design stage rather than mitigating harms afterwards. It proposes accountability, liability and oversight structures, and concludes that AI-generated religious rulings pose unacceptable risks to religious authority. The site also has a post on how Yaqeen approaches AI. Transferable method: fiqh al-muwazanat, a codified way of weighing harms against benefits, used as a design-stage AI assessment, delivered to a very large Muslim audience.

name: Nishan Forum on World Civilizations / Nishan World Center for Confucian Studies
one_line: A recurring forum on Confucianism and civilisational dialogue in Qufu, organised by the Nishan World Center for Confucian Studies (secretariat of the China Confucius Foundation) with the Shandong provincial government. In 2026 it ran a dedicated track on 'Artificial Intelligence and Universal Harmony'.
field_lens: Confucian philosophy (ren, yi, datong or 'universal harmony'); Daoist scholars also take part through the Laozi Research Institute
ai_connection: The 2026 forum (theme 'Civilization·Order·Justice', ending 29 Sep 2026, more than 340 participants from over 40 countries) made 'AI and universal harmony' a sub-topic with two breakout sessions. Organisers said it would offer Confucian value guidance, centred on ren (humaneness), for global AI governance. Speakers argued, for example, that yi (righteousness) 'demands upholding the moral baseline that distinguishes humanity from algorithms'. Transferable method: Confucian relational ethics and civilisational dialogue applied to AI governance norms. Caveat: the forum is state-linked, and only the 2026 edition's AI track was verified.

name: European Association for the Study of Science and Technology (EASST)
one_line: Europe's learned society for science and technology studies (STS), founded in 1981. It runs the biennial EASST conference, EASST Review and the EASST Fund.
field_lens: STS: ethnography, controversy mapping, sociotechnical imaginaries, critical AI studies
ai_connection: EASST2026 (Kraków, 8-11 Sept 2026, theme 'More Than Now: Exploring resilient futures') ran at least 16 AI panels. They include 'Ground truths and the epistemology of AI', 'The politics of machine learning (ML) evaluation', 'AI cold war and AI nationalism', 'A field in formation: what do we mean by critical and AI in Critical AI Studies?' and 'Futures and critical AI literacies: resisting inevitability narratives'. The 2026 EASST Fund also backed a project on Iberoamerican imaginaries of AI. What it could lend AI safety: STS studies of how evaluation and benchmarking actually work in practice, and of how stories about the future steer AI development.

name: Society for Social Studies of Science (4S)
one_line: The main international STS society. It publishes Science, Technology & Human Values and the journal ESTS, and holds an annual meeting.
field_lens: STS, anthropology and history of science and technology
ai_connection: The 50th-anniversary meeting (Toronto, Oct 2026) is themed 'TechnoPower · Technoscientific Futures'. More than 30 of the roughly 250 accepted open panels are about AI, among them 'Polycentric Futures: Governing AI Beyond Monocentric Control', 'Contesting AI Futures: Grassroots Interventions and Alternative Imaginaries', 'AI Governance and Public Policy' and 'The Agency and Politics of LLM-Based Chatbots'. Plenary speakers include an anthropologist writing an ethnography of generative AI and a historian of technology who studies how environmental and existential-risk talk about AI connect. This is the largest gathering of people able to study AI-safety communities and their claims the way STS studies other sciences.

name: EPIC (Ethnographic Praxis in Industry Community)
one_line: A global nonprofit community for ethnographers working in business and organisations. It runs the annual EPIC conference, trainings and a case-study library.
field_lens: Applied anthropology and ethnography in industry
ai_connection: In 2026 its site featured 'Grounded Models: The Future of Sensemaking in a World of Generative AI', 'Decolonizing LLMs: An Ethnographic Framework for AI in African Contexts' and 'AI Tools in Humanistic & Social Research'. EPIC2026 (Chicago and online) is themed 'Modeling, predicting, and interpreting context'. Its members are practising ethnographers inside tech companies, so EPIC holds the method most needed to study AI labs and deployment contexts from the inside.

name: CASTAC (Committee on the Anthropology of Science, Technology and Computing), American Anthropological Association, incl. the Platypus blog
one_line: The American Anthropological Association's committee for anthropologists of science, technology and computing. It runs the Platypus blog, the Platypod podcast and a membership directory.
field_lens: Anthropology of science, technology and computing
ai_connection: Platypus keeps an AI tag and publishes ethnographic pieces on AI regularly. Examples: 'Automating Language, Losing Relationality: Feminist Reflections on African Language AI' (Jul 2026), 'The Kids Are AI-right' (Aug 2026), 'The Human Cost of Precision' (Mar 2026) and 'The Brilliant Future of AI' (2024). It is the organised home of anthropologists of computing in the US, and the natural partner for fieldwork on AI-safety and AI-lab cultures.

name: URPP Digital Religion(s), University of Zurich (incl. MEEET Lab)
one_line: A University Research Priority Program at the University of Zurich on religion in digital society, co-directed by the anthropologist of AI Beth Singler. The MEEET Lab (Media Existential Encounters and Evolving Technology) runs alongside it.
field_lens: Digital and social anthropology, religious studies: AI hopes, fears, apocalypticism and AI-as-religion
ai_connection: The URPP covers the ethics of transhumanism and AI, and co-hosted the 'Church & AI' conference (June 2026). Its MEEET Lab (funded 2023 to 2026) studies the benefits and the ethical, political, regulatory and health risks of AI with ethnographic methods. In 2025 the lab hosted the conference 'AI Hopes, Fears, and Realities'. Singler's ethnographic work covers AI apocalypticism and beliefs about AI sentience. It is one of the few institutional homes for ethnography of AI hope and doom, including AI-risk discourse.

name: Science, Technology, and Social Values Lab (ST&SV Lab), Institute for Advanced Study
one_line: Alondra Nelson's STS lab at IAS Princeton. It runs an AI Policy and Governance Working Group, the SINAI imaginaries project, AI and Geopolitics, and the AI Democracy Projects (with Proof News).
field_lens: STS and the social history of science: sociotechnical imaginaries and narratives
ai_connection: The AI Policy and Governance Working Group is a deliberately small group of experts with differing views who aim for rough consensus on high-priority AI policy issues. SINAI (Sociotechnical Imaginaries and Narratives of AI) traces how hopes and fears about AI, from automata to 'sentient' machines, shape legislation and forecasts. That makes SINAI a history-of-AI-hopes-and-fears project of the kind this sub-angle looks for. The AI Democracy Projects test generative AI on election information.

name: médialab, Sciences Po
one_line: An interdisciplinary STS and digital-methods lab founded in Bruno Latour's tradition. It works on controversy mapping and digital methods.
field_lens: STS, controversy mapping, digital methods, ethnography of practices
ai_connection: It has a research line on LLMs in ordinary work practice ('Écologies des pratiques LLMs'), and in 2026 co-ran seminars on agentic economies with Koray Caliskan and Donald MacKenzie, and on AI agents in advertising. It also releases its own LLM research framework (Spinosa). It was the French partner in Shaping AI, which mapped AI controversies. Controversy mapping could be applied to safety debates themselves. Based in Paris, where int/a has a community.

name: Shaping AI (Shaping 21st-Century AI: controversies and closure in media, policy and research)
one_line: A comparative STS project in four countries, funded through the European Open Research Area (Feb 2021 to Feb 2024). It mapped AI controversies in media, policy, research and public participation.
field_lens: STS controversy analysis; qualitative and comparative social research
ai_connection: It mapped how AI was built up as a scientific paradigm and a contested political reality in the UK, France, Germany and Canada. Its main event was the 'Shifting AI Controversies' conference (WZB Berlin, Jan 2024). Outputs include 'Reclaiming AI accounts: a plea for a participatory turn in AI inquiries' and the EASST-4S 2024 panel 'Rebooting the STS programme for AI'. Teams: Warwick CIM, Sciences Po médialab, ZeMKI Bremen with HIIG, and Concordia/INRS. It provides a ready method and dataset for studying how AI-risk controversies form and settle.

name: AIMODELS: The Culture of Algorithmic Models (ERC project, Ca' Foscari University of Venice)
one_line: An ERC project led by Matteo Pasquinelli (2024 to 2028) on the historical epistemology of AI. It studies the combined social and technical history of AI models and of models of intelligence.
field_lens: History and historical epistemology of science and technology; history of the measurement of labour and intelligence
ai_connection: It sets out to historicise AI through the history of modelling, from psychometrics and the IQ test to statistics and linguistics. It explicitly targets the anthropomorphism of AI and 'myths of superintelligence', and runs symposia, publications and a network. This is a critical historical counterpoint to AI-risk framings, useful for testing where the field's assumptions about intelligence come from.

name: Histories of Artificial Intelligence: A Genealogy of Power (Cambridge HPS, Mellon Sawyer Seminar)
one_line: An 18-month Sawyer Seminar at Cambridge's Department of History and Philosophy of Science on AI's history from antiquity to the present. Organisers included Stephanie Dick, Jonnie Penn, Sarah Dillon, Matthew Jones and Syed Mustafa Ali.
field_lens: History of science and technology, genealogy, critical race and gender studies
ai_connection: It traced how AI is entangled with politics, power and control through four threads: hidden labour, encoded behaviour, disingenuous rhetoric and cognitive injustice. It produced a model syllabus, a community bibliography (2020), methods training, research awards and a session on the history of connectionism. Its network of AI historians is the obvious pool for a history of AI-risk ideas. The site is still up, but the seminar itself has ended.

name: Center for Genetics and Society (CGS)
one_line: A Berkeley nonprofit, active for decades on the social-justice governance of human genetic technologies: germline editing, eugenics and assisted reproduction. It publishes Biopolitical Times.
field_lens: Biotech governance, bioethics, history of eugenics and techno-utopianism
ai_connection: It now covers AI in its commentary: 'Is AI the End of the World as We Know It?' (Biopolitical Times, Sept 2026) and a running archive on AI risk statements and deregulation. What it could lend: decades of public-interest experience governing a powerful dual-use technology (heritable genome editing), and a historical critique of eugenic and transhumanist ideas that overlap with AI-future debates.

name: Deutsches Museum Research Institute (Forschungsinstitut für Technik- und Wissenschaftsgeschichte)
one_line: The Deutsches Museum's research institute for the history of science and technology. One research area is 'Digitale Technik- und Wissenskulturen' (digital technology and knowledge cultures).
field_lens: History of technology and science; museology; feminist epistemology
ai_connection: Current projects: 'Ethik der autonomen Fahrzeuge', which uses feminist epistemology to work out how ethical questions get into the sociotechnical development of autonomous vehicles, five years after the first pedestrian death; 'Artificial Vision at Work', a history of automating vision; and the 21-year 'Edition Wissenschaftliche Software' (2026 to 2046) on preserving the history of scientific software. What it could lend: a historian's long view and archival care for safety-critical autonomy.

name: BlackboxNLP: Workshop on Analyzing and Interpreting Neural Networks for NLP
location: Moves with EMNLP (2025 Suzhou, 2026 Budapest); organisers at Technion, Boston University, Groningen, Tilburg and elsewhere
one_line: Annual interpretability workshop, running since 2018 and held alongside EMNLP. The ninth edition is in Budapest on 29 October 2026, with a reproducibility challenge.
field_lens: Computational linguistics and psycholinguistics, alongside psychology and neuroscience. It explicitly brings linguistic analysis to the question of what language models represent. MISFIT: the taxonomy has no linguistics tradition, so it is placed under psych_cognitive.
ai_connection: It is the main place where linguists study language-model internals: probing representations, inductive biases and what makes a model interpretable. This is a standing outlet for interpretability, an AI-safety agenda, approached through linguistics rather than mainstream ML alignment.

name: Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL): Ethics Committee, Code of Ethics and Responsible NLP Research Checklist
location: International society, registered in the US
one_line: The ACL is the learned society of computational linguistics. It adopted a code of ethics in 2020, and the Ethics Committee helped shape the Responsible NLP checklist that every ARR submission must complete (revised for the October 2024 cycle).
